payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the image into pencil drawing
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Are the scene's tonal modeling and reflections broadly represented as pencil-drawn shading rather than retained photographic rendering?
node.criteria: Pass if pencil-rendered tonal values broadly convey volume, lighting and reflective surfaces through stroke-density modeling, hatching, form-following graphite shading or convincing rubbed graphite tones. Smooth shading, preserved lighting geometry and retained color are compatible with pencil drawing when the tonal transitions themselves visibly read as drawing material. Evaluate whether graphite-like density and blending articulate light-to-dark transitions, rather than merely overlaying unchanged photographic tones. Fail if substantial surfaces retain photographic tonal modeling or specular rendering beneath added noise or strokes. Desaturation, softened contrast, stronger contours and grain alone are insufficient. Isolated realistic highlights or imperfect surfaces do not establish failure when pencil-rendered modeling is broadly established; conversely, isolated converted patches do not establish satisfaction. Assess tonal representation independently of contour quality and the mere presence of surface marks. Use unknown only when the visual evidence cannot establish the tonal-rendering style.
node.binding: Compare the supplied SOURCE and EDITED images against the requested pencil-drawing transformation. Independently judge this tonal-rendering condition as pass, fail or unknown. Compare corresponding regions of the sprouts and carrots, potato slices and shaded food, plate and table, and pitcher and wine glass. Examine whether source highlights, midtones and shadows have become coherent graphite-like value structures: look for drawing-material density, blended graphite transitions or strokes that actually model volume, not simply texture laid over photographic gradients. Explicitly examine the edited sprouts' light-to-dark transitions, shaded food and plate alongside the pitcher and wine glass highlights. Identify concrete evidence supporting conversion and any substantial regions retaining photographic modeling, then assess their distribution across the scene. Do not classify a transition as photographic solely because it is smooth or follows the source lighting; explain which visible properties distinguish it from smooth rubbed graphite. Do not classify a transition as pencil-rendered solely because it is desaturated, softened or grainy. Remaining glassware highlights are relevant evidence but are not automatically dispositive, and progress elsewhere does not by itself satisfy this condition. Cite the tonal characteristics supporting the judgment. Use unknown only for genuinely insufficient visual evidence, not low confidence or disagreement. The target is pencil-drawn representation of the image's visual content; the reference is the supplied image and the requested pencil-drawing transformation.

node_traces.evidence: The edit is desaturated and grainy, but much of the scene retains photographic tonal modeling. The sprouts and carrots still show smooth, source-like light-to-dark gradients and glossy highlights rather than graphite strokes or blended pencil shading that clearly models their forms. The shaded food and potato slices likewise retain photographic-looking highlights and shadows, while the plate and table mostly preserve smooth tonal transitions with texture overlaid. The pitcher and wine glass retain smooth reflective highlights and gradients. These characteristics are substantial across the scene; the added grain and softened contrast do not establish pencil-rendered tonal modeling.
